lead: A Boolean algebra is a lattice with three extra powers: it has a smallest element 0 and a largest element 1, meet distributes over join (and join over meet), and every element a has a complement a′ with a∨a′=1 and a∧a′=0. This short set of laws is enough to prove the usual rules of sets and logic. Circuit designers use it to simplify gates; database engineers use it to rewrite conditions; students meet it in truth tables and set identities. Its two definitions—order-based and equation-based—are equivalent.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.4 for bounded, complemented and distributive lattices.

blocks.text: A Boolean algebra can be described in two equivalent ways. The first uses order. Start with a lattice (B,∨,∧). It is bounded: there are elements 0 and 1 with 0≤a≤1 for all a. It is distributive: meet distributes over join and join over meet. It is complemented: for each a there is a′ with a∨a′=1 and a∧a′=0. A lattice with all four properties is a Boolean algebra, and we require 0≠1. The second description forgets order and lists equations. Let B be a set with two operations ∨ and ∧, one unary operation ′, and constants 0 and 1. For all a,b,c∈B the commutative, distributive, identity and complement laws hold, and 0≠1. The two descriptions match: from the lattice conditions you get the equations, and from the equations you can define a≤b iff a∨b=b and recover a bounded distributive complemented lattice. Some books call the equation list Huntington's postulates. Some syllabi write + and · for ∨ and ∧, but ∨ and ∧ keep the lattice connection clear.

blocks.where: a, b, c are elements of B; ∨ is join; ∧ is meet; ′ is complement; 0 and 1 are the bounds.

blocks.text: From the compact list many familiar laws follow. Idempotent: a∨a=a and a∧a=a. Proof: a∨a=(a∨a)∧1=(a∨a)∧(a∨a′)=a∨(a∧a′)=a∨0=a. Bounded laws: a∨0=a, a∧0=0, a∨1=1, a∧1=a. Absorption: a∨(a∧b)=a and a∧(a∨b)=a. Involution: (a′)′=a. De Morgan: (a∨b)′=a′∧b′ and (a∧b)′=a′∨b′. These are theorems, not extra assumptions. A quick way to prove De Morgan is to show that a′∧b′ is the complement of a∨b: (a∨b)∨(a′∧b′)=1 and (a∨b)∧(a′∧b′)=0, then use uniqueness of complement. Complement is unique: if x and y both satisfy a∨x=1, a∧x=0, a∨y=1, a∧y=0, then x=x∧1=x∧(a∨y)=(x∧a)∨(x∧y)=0∨(x∧y)=x∧y, and similarly y=x∧y, so x=y. Duality: any true identity remains true when ∨ and ∧ are swapped and 0 and 1 are swapped. Example: a∨(a∧b)=a duals to a∧(a∨b)=a.

The smallest Boolean algebra is B2={0,1}. Join is max, meet is min, and complement is 1−a: 0′=1, 1′=0. The power set P(S) of any set S is a Boolean algebra: join is union, meet is intersection, complement is S−A, zero is ∅ and one is S. For S={1,2,3}, take A={1,2} and C={2,3}. Then A∨C={1,2,3}, A∧C={2}, A′={3}, C′={1}. De Morgan holds: (A∨C)′=∅ and A′∧C′={3}∩{1}=∅. Also A∨A′={1,2,3} and A∧A′=∅, so A′ is the complement of A. The order in P(S) is subset: A≤C means A⊆C. The same algebra appears in logic: ∨ is OR, ∧ is AND, ′ is NOT, 0 is false, 1 is true. Duality says swapping ∨ with ∧ and 0 with 1 turns a valid law into another valid law. Complement uniqueness is why the notation a′ is safe. Boolean polynomials and normal forms use these laws in Chapter 5.6.

examples.question: Let U={1,2,3} and B=P(U). Let A={1,2} and C={2,3}. In the Boolean algebra (B,∪,∩,′,∅,U), compute A∨C, A∧C, A′, C′. Then verify De Morgan's law (A∨C)′=A′∧C′ and the complement law A∨A′=U. Give the sizes of the six sets A∨C, A∧C, A′, C′, (A∨C)′ and A′∧C′.
steps: A′∧C′={3}∩{1}=∅; size 0. Hence De Morgan holds.
A∨A′={1,2}∪{3}=U and A∧A′=∅, so A′ is complement of A.
examples.answer: The six sizes are 3, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0; De Morgan's law and the complement law hold.

traps: Mixing the distributive laws. The correct law is a∨(b∧c)=(a∨b)∧(a∨c). Writing (a∨b)∧c leaves c outside the first bracket.
Forgetting 0≠1. A one-element set {0} with 0=1 fails the definition.
Using the wrong De Morgan law. (a∨b)′=a′∧b′, not a′∨b′.
Assuming a complemented bounded lattice is automatically Boolean. Distributivity is also required; the diamond lattice is complemented but not distributive.
Believing complements can be many. In a Boolean algebra each a has exactly one complement a′.

quiz.q: State the two complement laws and the condition linking 0 and 1.
quiz.a: a∨a′=1 and a∧a′=0 for every a in B; also 0≠1.

quiz.q: Why is B2={0,1} a Boolean algebra? Give join, meet and complement.
quiz.a: Join is max, meet is min, complement is 1−a; the laws hold and 0≠1.

quiz.q: In P({1,2,3}) with A={1,3} and B={2,3}, compute A∨B, A∧B, A′, B′ and check (A∧B)′=A′∨B′.
Prove that the complement of an element a in a Boolean algebra is unique.
quiz.a: If x and y are complements of a, then x=x∧1=x∧(a∨y)=(x∧a)∨(x∧y)=0∨(x∧y)=x∧y, and similarly y=x∧y. Hence x=y.

quiz.q: State the duality principle and give the dual of a∧(a∨b)=a.
quiz.a: Swap ∨ with ∧ and 0 with 1; the dual is a∨(a∧b)=a.

quiz.q: Use absorption to simplify a∨(a∧b) and (a∨b)∧a.
Give a complemented bounded lattice that is not distributive, and show which distributive law fails.
quiz.a: Diamond M3 with 0,1 and atoms a,b,c. It is complemented but not distributive: a∧(b∨c)=a∧1=a, while (a∧b)∨(a∧c)=0∨0=0. So a∧(b∨c)≠(a∧b)∨(a∧c).

beyond: Not for the exam. Boolean algebras sit under switching circuits and SAT solvers: a clause is a join of literals, and simplifying clauses is algebra. Database query optimizers use the same identities to reorder filters and joins. In advanced mathematics, Stone's representation theorem says every Boolean algebra is a field of sets. Search for Boolean algebra, Stone representation theorem, and SAT solver clause simplification.
